sources.citation: Hossaini, Khadija & Thomas Ruttig. 2019. Citizens, Finally, But No Place to Settle: The Magats, one of Afghanistan's most marginalised minorities. Kabul: Afghanistan Analysts Network (AAN report, Context & Culture series; ecoi.net document 2036107).
sources.note: No phonology. Says Magati is a 'secret language' on a Persian/Dari base with borrowed vocabulary (after Pstrusinska) and that Guenther called it 'defamiliarised [modified] Tajiki' used only for dissociation in public, families otherwise speaking Tajiki/Persian/Pashto; the only 'stress' remark is about the ethnonym ('The Magat (with stress on the first syllable, ie pronounced Mágat)'), not about word stress in the register.

sources.citation: Pstrusińska, Jadwiga. 2013. Secret Languages of Afghanistan and Their Speakers. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing. ISBN 978-1-4438-4970-8. (30-page publisher sample: front matter, Introduction pp.1-16, start of ch.1)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. sources.citation: Pstrusińska, Jadwiga. 2009. O idei tajnych języków Afganistanu. Kraków: Wydawnictwo Uniwersytetu Jagiellońskiego (4-page chapter; RUJ item 78588; CORE 64747552).
sources.note: no phonology content; historical-comparative remarks on argot vocabulary (Kitab-i Sasian parallels, bazaar diffusion) and the hybrid-language characterisation only.

sources.citation: Jasiewicz, Zbigniew. 2005. [Review article on] Jadwiga Pstrusińska, O tajnych językach Afganistanu i ich użytkownikach, Księgarnia Akademicka, Kraków 2004, ss. 166. Etnografia Polska 49: 253-256.
sources.note: Secondhand description of the 2004 book's contents: definitions of secret language, ethnolinguistic situation of Afghanistan, the discovery of magati by the Poznan ethnologists, a register of 13 Afghan secret languages, modes of encoding, lexical resources and 'borrowed grammatical bases'; treats the argots as essentially lexical (cites Oranskij's 'secret vocabularies'); observes magati was to some extent used group-internally by all generations among the Hajdars. Nothing on pronunciation, stress or tone; confirms the 2004/2013 books are not phonological descriptions.

sources.citation: Windfuhr, Gernot L. 2002 (last updated 2012). GYPSY ii. Gypsy Dialects. Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XI, Fasc. 4, pp. 415-421. New York: Encyclopaedia Iranica Foundation.
sources.note: Nothing. Linguistic content is Domari/Lomavren/Romani historical sound changes, Para-Romani-type restructuring ('All Gypsy languages are typologically hybrids..'), and Fiuj-Gorbati word-disguise devices; for the Afghan Persian-based groups it only names languages and cites Rao 1995 and Pstrusinska 1986. 0 hits for stress/accent.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1995. Marginality and language use: the example of peripatetics in Afghanistan. Journal of the Gypsy Lore Society, Series 5, 5(2): 69-95.
sources.note: Explicitly declines to mark accentuation/stress; gives a 15-item list of Mogatibey substantives (dalxak 'girl', dawa 'horse', daya 'father', mamgis 'mother', nuhur 'eye', etc.) with etymological notes linking them to Central Asian Lyuli/Jugi argot (Oranskij 1983) and Gorbati; characterises the Jogi tongue as an artificial (secret) language on a Persian substratum; the only phonological content in the paper concerns Gorbati (phoneme substitution, m- prefixation), not Magati. Wordlist-plus-sociolinguistics, no prosody.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1994. Peripatetics of Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkey. In John Middleton & Amal Rassam (eds.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures, vol. IX: Africa and the Middle East, 274-276. Boston: G. K. Hall. (Glottolog ref 326078; read in the encyclopedia.com reprint.)

sources.citation: Pstrusińska, Jadwiga. 1986. Magati: some notes on an unknown language of northern Afghanistan. Journal of the Anthropological Society of Oxford 17(2): 135-139.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the 5 pages. The only linguistic data is a 31-item wordlist and 13 sentences gathered by Z. Jasiewicz and A. Ananicz in 1976, reproduced 'exactly as received (and transcribed, moreover, according to the rules of Polish orthography)' (p.136), with no stress marks; p.138: 'the grammatical system was very similar to that of a Persian dialect, whereas the vocabulary seemed to be of mixed origin'; p.136: speakers use 'Persian (in its local Dari version)' with outsiders and also know Uzbek. Open-access scan from Oxford ORA (scanned text).

sources.citation: Kieffer, Charles M. 1983 (updated 2011). AFGHANISTAN v. Languages. Encyclopaedia Iranica I/5: 501-516, section 32 (Jat argots).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Says: 'Magatibai is the language of the Jōgī, who move about in the provinces of Balḵ, Jōzǰān, Fāryāb, and Kondūz. Part of its vocabulary is shared by Magadī of the Ḡorbat (see A. Rao, Note préliminaire sur les Jat d'Afghanistan, Studia Iranica 8, 1979, p. 144)'; the Jat argots are 'structurally Iranian'. Internet Archive copy held under (live iranicaonline.org could not be reached by automated download).

sources.citation: Kieffer, Charles M. 1986 (cited in Pstrusińska 2013:3 n., p.103, listing 'ādūrgarī; qazūlagī or magadī, or ġorbatī, and.. magatibai (under research)').

sources.note: Kieffer is the Afghan-Persian phonetician of record; his classification of the Jat argots as 'structurally Iranian' is the closest thing to a phonological characterisation; the 1986 item's full reference was not visible in the sample.
